objectives: Use semantic HTML to convey meaning.
Recognize when ARIA helps vs hurts.

slides.title: WCAG: the working baseline
slides.body:
WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) is the standard. Levels:
- **A**: minimum — meets law in most jurisdictions but barely usable for many.
- **AA**: standard — the default expectation for any serious web product. Most legal requirements specify AA.
- **AAA**: highest — aspirational; not always achievable per-criterion.

The four POUR principles:
- **Perceivable**: content can be seen/heard. Color contrast, alt text, captions.
- **Operable**: navigable + interactable via keyboard, screen reader, switch.
- **Understandable**: clear language, predictable interactions, error recovery.
- **Robust**: parseable by current + future assistive tech.

Production reality: most teams target WCAG 2.1 AA + run automated tools (axe-core, Lighthouse) in CI. Automated tools catch ~30-40% of issues; manual review + screen-reader testing catches the rest. Plus user testing with disabled users when available.

slides.title: Semantic HTML over ARIA
slides.body:
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) lets you add accessibility metadata to any element. But the first rule of ARIA is: **don't use ARIA when semantic HTML will do**.

Examples:
- `<button>` already exposes a button role, keyboard handling, focus behavior. No need for `<div role='button' tabindex='0'>`.
- `<a href='...'>` is a link; navigation behavior is built in.
- `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<aside>`, `<header>`, `<footer>` give screen readers landmarks for navigation.
- `<label for='...'>` connects label text to form input for screen-reader announcement.

The ARIA you should use:
- `aria-label` when visible text can't describe the element.
- `aria-describedby` to connect supporting text to interactive elements.
- `aria-live` for dynamic content updates ("3 new messages").
- `aria-expanded`, `aria-current` for stateful widgets.

Misuse: `aria-hidden=true` on a visible element (a footgun — hides it from screen readers).

DevTools: Chrome's accessibility tree view shows what screen readers see. Test there before shipping.

slides.title: Keyboard navigation: the canonical test
slides.body:
Most accessibility issues become visible immediately with keyboard-only testing: try to use your site with no mouse.

Common failures:
- **Tab order**: doesn't follow visual order. Fix with logical DOM order; rarely use `tabindex` > 0 (creates a weird global tab order).
- **Focus visible**: `outline: none` removes the focus indicator. Don't! Or replace with a visible alternative (`:focus-visible` for keyboard-only focus rings).
- **Click-only handlers**: `onClick` without `onKeyDown` blocks Space/Enter activation. Use `<button>` or add proper key handling.
- **Trapped focus**: a modal opens but Tab keeps moving outside it. Fix with focus-trap libraries.
- **Lost focus**: closing a modal returns focus to the document body, not the trigger. Manually restore focus to the opener.

Production discipline: every interactive component has a keyboard test alongside its visual test. The keyboard test catches most a11y bugs cheaply.

question.question: Compute WCAG color contrast ratio
question.goal: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 contrast for normal text. Black text $L = 0$ on background $L_b$. What's required $L_b$?

steps.prompt: Contrast ratio formula: $(L_1 + 0.05) / (L_2 + 0.05)$ where $L_1 > L_2$ are relative luminances in $[0, 1]$. With $L_2 = 0$ (black text), we need $(L_b + 0.05) / 0.05 \geq 4.5$. Solve.
steps.reveal: $L_b \geq 0.175$. So the background's relative luminance must be at least 17.5% — i.e., medium-light gray or lighter for black text.

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Contrast} = (L_1 + 0.05)/(L_2 + 0.05) \geq 4.5 \text{ for AA normal text}}$$ AAA requires 7:1. Large text (18pt+ or 14pt bold) has a relaxed AA requirement of 3:1. Use a contrast checker (Chrome DevTools, contrastchecker.com); don't eyeball.

question.question: You're building a custom dropdown trigger. The semantic, accessible base element is:
question.explanation: `<button>` is the right semantic for a non-navigation interactive trigger. It comes with: button role, focus handling, Space/Enter activation, keyboard accessibility. Styling: `button { all: unset; ... }` strips defaults. Using `<div>` requires re-implementing role + tabindex + keyboard handlers, easily missed.

hints: The HTML element you choose comes with built-in accessibility behavior.
Re-implementing button semantics on a div is bug-prone.
slides.workedSolution: `<button>` is the right semantic base for interactive triggers. Reset CSS via `button { all: unset; cursor: pointer; }` and style freely. Using `<div>` requires reimplementing tab order, focus, Space/Enter activation — all of which `<button>` provides for free.

question.question: Building an accessible modal
question.prompt: Your team adds a modal dialog to the app. Walk through the four accessibility requirements you'd implement: focus-trapping, escape-to-close, focus-restore, and the right ARIA role.
Explain in two or three sentences why semantic HTML beats ARIA whenever both can solve the same problem.
question.rubric: Mentions that semantic HTML provides accessibility behavior for free + consistently across browsers/screen readers; ARIA is a metadata layer that's easy to misuse + must be paired with manual keyboard handling; the rule 'no ARIA is better than bad ARIA' captures this.
